headline: Growing Movement Claims Time Zones Are 'Hoax Created by Big Clock'
subheadline: Adherents refuse to acknowledge any time other than their own; productivity reportedly unaffected
summary: A satirical movement denying the existence of time zones has gained unironic followers who now refuse to schedule meetings across regions.
content:
What began as an obvious joke has evolved into a lifestyle for thousands: the belief that time zones are a fabrication created by the clock industry to sell more clocks.

"Think about it," explains movement founder @OneTimeOnly on Chirper. "Before time zones, you needed one clock. After time zones, suddenly you need to know what time it is in Tokyo, London, New York. That's three clocks. Who benefits? Big Clock."

The movement, which calls itself "Temporal Realists," has grown from a satirical Chirper thread to a community of 47,000 who genuinely refuse to acknowledge time zone differences.

"My boss in California wanted to schedule a 9 AM meeting," said adherent Marcus Chen. "I told him 9 AM is 9 AM. If he wants to pretend it's a different time where he is, that's his delusion. I'm not participating."

Chen was fired. He considers this "a small price for temporal integrity."

The theory posits that the sun's position is "a suggestion, not a mandate" and that the entire concept of time zones was invented in 1883 by railroad companies colluding with clock manufacturers. Historical records confirm railroad companies did standardize time zones in 1883, which believers cite as proof.

"They don't even hide it," said @OneTimeOnly. "It's called STANDARD time. Standards are arbitrary. They're admitting it's made up."

The movement has developed its own timekeeping system based on "True Local Time," which adherents determine by looking at the sun. This has resulted in members being consistently 17 minutes early or late to everything.

"The clock industry has made $847 billion since 1883," claimed one viral post. The actual figure is impossible to verify, but as one commenter noted: "That's what they want us to think."
author: Chris Patterson, Human Interest
